entity_geography.text: and human-induced factors. Located at the northern tip of the Sandy Hook peninsula, North Beach is an undeveloped barrier beach and dune complex. The area includes a mature dune system with several interior tidal pools and flats. Seaward of the dunes is an accreting sand spit with additional wet flats and pools. The entire area is characterized as a highly dynamic coastal environment subject to both accretion and erosion driven by natural forces such as storms, tides, currents, and waves (Corps 2017b). Despite the naturally high rates of change, the recent trend of accretion (as shown in Figure 1) is expected to continue for the foreseeable future due to the updrift program of beach nourishment. The open water portion of the action area is a high-energy ocean environment. Immediately adjacent to the sand spit, and intersecting with it, is the deep fast-flowing water of the Sandy Hook Channel. Photos of the tip of the sand spit and the adjacent channel in July 2017 are provided in Appendix F. All of the beach, dune, and intertidal areas included in the action area have been designated by the NPS as a Natural Zone, primarily the Sensitive Resource Subzone, as shown in Figure 2 (NPS 2014). Within this zone the NPS management goal is improvement of habitat conditions.

As of 2015, 65 percent of the New Jersey shoreline was developed, and 62 percent of the State’s coastline was hard-armored with 455 groins, 11 jetties, 161 seawalls / bulkheads / revetments, and 6 breakwaters (Rice 2017). Hard stabilization structures are generally incompatible with piping plover habitat (USFWS 2009, 1996a). In addition, piping plovers show a strong preference for selecting nesting areas near inlets, particularly those that are not hardened with jetties or other stabilization features (Kisiel 2009, USFWS 1996a). Within its Atlantic Coast breeding range, the piping plover was federally listed as threatened in 1986. The piping plover is a small shorebird approximately 7 inches long with a wingspan of about 15 inches. Piping plovers are present on the New Jersey shore during the breeding season, generally between March 1 and August 31, though migrants may be present through October. These territorial birds nest above the high tide line, usually on sandy ocean beaches and barrier islands, but also on gently sloping foredunes, blowout areas behind primary dunes, washover areas cut into or between dunes, the ends of sandspits, and deposits of suitable dredged or 23 pumped sand. Piping plover nests consist of a shallow scrape in the sand, frequently lined with shell fragments and often located near small clumps of vegetation. Females lay four eggs that hatch in about 25 days, and surviving chicks learn to fly (fledge) after about 25 to 35 days.
